title: Occupational safety and health
description: Field concerned with the safety, health and welfare of people at work
wiki_lead:
Occupational safety and health (OSH) or occupational health and safety (OHS) is a multidisciplinary field concerned with the safety, health, and welfare of people at work (i.e., while performing duties required by one's occupation). OSH is related to the fields of occupational medicine and occupational hygiene and aligns with workplace health promotion initiatives. OSH also protects all the general public who may be affected by the occupational environment.
According to the official estimates of the United Nations, the WHO/ILO Joint Estimate of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury, almost 2 million people die each year due to exposure to occupational risk factors. Globally, more than 2.78 million people die annually as a result of workplace-related accidents or diseases, corresponding to one death every fifteen seconds. There are an additional 374 million non-fatal work-related injuries annually. It is estimated that the economic burden of occupational-related injury and death is nearly four per cent of the global gross domestic product each year. The human cost of this adversity is enormous.
In common-law jurisdictions, employers have the common law duty (also called duty of care) to take reasonable care of the safety of their employees. Statute law may, in addition, impose other general duties, introduce specific duties, and create government bodies with powers to regulate occupational safety issues. Details of this vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.
Prevention of workplace incidents and occupational diseases is addressed through the implementation of occupational safety and health programs at company level.

Definitions
The International Labour Organization (ILO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) share a common definition of occupational health. It was first adopted by the Joint ILO/WHO Committee on Occupational Health at its first session in 1950:

Occupational health should aim at the promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations; the prevention amongst workers of departures from health caused by their working conditions; the protection of workers in their employment from risks resulting from factors adverse to health; the placing and maintenance of the worker in an occupational environment adapted to his physiological and psychological capabilities and; to summarize: the adaptation of work to man and of each man to his job.
In 1995, a consensus statement was added:

Occupational health focuses on three different objectives: (i) the maintenance and promotion of workers' health and working capacity; (ii) the improvement of working environment and work to become conducive to safety and health and (iii) development of work organizations and working cultures in a direction which supports health and safety at work and in doing so also promotes a positive social climate and smooth operation and may enhance productivity of the undertakings. The concept of working culture is intended in this context to mean a reflection of the essential value systems adopted by the undertaking concerned. grok_lead: Occupational safety and health (OSH), also known as occupational health and safety, is a multidisciplinary field focused on the prevention of work-related injuries, diseases, and fatalities through the systematic identification, evaluation, and mitigation of workplace hazards, including physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, and psychosocial risks. It integrates engineering controls, administrative policies, personal protective equipment, worker training, and regulatory enforcement to foster safe working environments, drawing on empirical evidence from epidemiology, toxicology, and industrial hygiene to establish causal links between exposures and health outcomes. Globally, occupational hazards result in approximately 2.93 million worker deaths annually, with work-related diseasesâsuch as respiratory illnesses from dust and chemicals, cancers from carcinogens, and cardiovascular conditions exacerbated by stressâaccounting for over 80% of these fatalities, far outpacing injuries from accidents. Additionally, around 395 million workers endure non-fatal injuries each year, leading to lost productivity, medical costs, and long-term disabilities, with the highest burdens concentrated in agriculture, construction, and manufacturing sectors in low- and middle-income countries where informal employment predominates. Key historical milestones include Bernardino Ramazzini's 1700 treatise De Morbis Artificum Diatriba, which pioneered systematic observation of occupation-specific diseases, and the establishment of modern regulatory frameworks, such as the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, which created the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and led to a substantial reduction in U.S. workplace fatality rates from 18 per 100,000 full-time workers in 1970 to 3.3 in 2023. Similar advancements in Europe and elsewhere, driven by International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions since 1919, have halved injury rates in compliant jurisdictions through mandatory standards and inspections, though effectiveness hinges on rigorous enforcement and adaptation to emerging risks like nanotechnology and shift work. Despite these gains, controversies persist regarding regulatory efficacy, as empirical analyses reveal that while penalties and inspections deter violations and reduce incidents, overly prescriptive rules can yield diminishing returns by increasing compliance burdens without proportionally addressing root causes, particularly in small enterprises or regions with weak labor inspections. Underreporting, economic incentives to prioritize output over safeguards, and gaps in addressing chronic disease causationâevident in persistent exposures to known hazards like silica dustâunderscore ongoing challenges, with data from international bodies indicating that voluntary management systems often outperform mandatory ones only when paired with accountability mechanisms.
